questions.stem: You have taken over a project replacing the appointment and stock system at an orthotics and prosthetics service. Your predecessor left three weeks ago. What the customer expects now exists as a folder of two hundred emails, a spreadsheet of agreed items carrying no dates, and a clinical lead who says the important things were settled in corridor conversations. The steering group meets in a fortnight. What should you do first?

options.text: Reconstruct the expectation list from the email folder and work to it, since the correspondence is contemporaneous evidence.
options.rationale: The error is treating a written trail as a shared understanding. Emails record what someone said at a moment, not what the other party took from it or whether it still stands nine months later.

options.text: Reconstruct the list, then take it to the clinical lead and the service manager to confirm, amend or strike each line before the steering group meets.
options.rationale: Reconstruction is the cheap half; confirmation is the half that makes the list the customer's rather than yours. Doing it before the steering group means you report an agreed position instead of an inherited one.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to reissue an authoritative requirements document so there is a single baseline to work from.
options.rationale: The error is answering a shared-understanding problem with an authority document. A baseline nobody has re-read tells you what was signed, not what the people who will use the system are currently expecting.

options.text: Report to the steering group that customer expectations are undocumented and ask for the project to pause while they are re-established.
options.rationale: The error is converting your own onboarding gap into a governance event. Two weeks is enough to do the confirming work, and a pause request spends credibility on something well within your control.

questions.explanation: A record of what a customer expects is a claim about the customer until the customer has seen it and agreed it. Reconstructing from correspondence establishes what was said, not what was understood or what still holds, and the gap between those surfaces at acceptance where it costs most. Confirmation is cheap while it is early and never becomes cheaper.
questions.mindset: An expectation you have written down but the customer has not confirmed is still only your assumption.

questions.stem: Your squad builds dispatch software for a cycle courier network. At the end of today's review, while people are collecting their coats, the operator's head dispatcher says she had assumed same-day route re-optimisation would be in place before the winter peak. It has never been discussed in refinement, it is nowhere in the backlog, and nobody wrote anything down. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Capture it as a backlog item today and tell her where it currently sits relative to the work already committed.
options.rationale: It makes an expectation visible without promising it, and telling her the position is what stops an unranked hope becoming an assumed delivery date. A remark made in passing is still information about what the customer is planning around.

options.text: Explain that route re-optimisation has never been in scope for this phase.
options.rationale: The error is answering an expectation with a scope statement. It is accurate and it closes the conversation, leaving you knowing less about why she expected it and what she has arranged on the strength of it.

options.text: Note it in your own notebook and raise it if she mentions it a second time.
options.rationale: The error is keeping a customer expectation in a private record. Waiting for a second mention means the first time you formally hear about it is likely to be the week she needed it.

options.text: Tell her the team can fit it in before winter, since re-optimisation is a small change to logic that already exists.
options.rationale: The error is committing on the spot to work the team has not sized or prioritised. A commitment made in a doorway becomes the thing she plans her peak season around.

questions.explanation: Expectations arrive far more often as asides than as requests, and the whole discipline is capturing them at the moment they surface rather than at the moment they are formally raised. Logging one costs nothing and commits nothing; the act that changes the relationship is telling the customer where it stands, because that is what lets them plan against reality rather than hope.
questions.mindset: Treat an aside about what someone assumed as data to be captured, not conversation to be answered.

questions.stem: A district heating scheme is being extended to 900 homes. Your contract is with the housing association that pays for the work and will own the network. The people who will judge whether it works are the residents, who expect warmth, quiet plant rooms and no billing surprises, and who have no contractual relationship with you at all. The two sets of expectations have already diverged over plant room siting. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Record the association and the residents as distinct customers with distinct expectations and distinct measures of success.
options.rationale: Naming them separately is what stops one set of expectations being quietly assumed to cover the other. Two customers with one entry in the register produces a plan that satisfies whichever of them wrote the entry.

options.text: Agree with the association how residents' expectations will be gathered and who decides when the two conflict.
options.rationale: The conflict is foreseeable and will recur, so the useful work is agreeing the mechanism once rather than negotiating each instance. It also keeps the paying customer inside a process you would otherwise be running around them.

options.text: Treat the housing association as the single voice of the customer, since it holds the contract and represents its tenants.
options.rationale: The error is collapsing the customer into the counterparty. The association can commit money and consent, but it cannot be dissatisfied on a resident's behalf, and dissatisfaction is what will define this scheme's reputation.

options.text: Survey residents directly on plant room siting and take the majority answer into the design.
options.rationale: The error is acting on the expectations of a group you have no mandate to satisfy, over the head of the customer who does. It also promises residents an influence you cannot guarantee to honour.

options.text: Defer resident engagement until commissioning, when there is something real to show them.
options.rationale: The error is deferring the group whose expectations take longest to move. By commissioning the siting decisions are made, so engagement becomes explanation and any expectation gap has hardened into a complaint.

questions.explanation: Where the paying customer and the judging customer are different people, both have to appear in the plan by name, and the recurring failure is assuming that a contract with one carries authority over the satisfaction of the other. The useful artefact is not a longer list of expectations but an agreed rule for whose expectation prevails when they collide, settled before the first collision rather than during it.
questions.mindset: The customer who pays and the customer who judges are two customers unless you have checked that they are one.

questions.stem: A freight forwarder is replacing the customs entry system its clerks have used for eleven years. The old system let a clerk save a half-finished entry and complete it later; the new one validates on save and will not accept an incomplete record. Three weeks after go-live the clerks have logged forty-one defect reports about this, all describing it as data being lost. The customs manager supports them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the reports as defects and change the new system to permit incomplete saves, restoring the behaviour the clerks relied on.
options.rationale: The error is treating familiarity as a requirement. Eleven years of a behaviour makes it expected, not correct, and reinstating it without knowing what it was used for may reinstate the problem the validation was specified to solve.

options.text: Explain that validation on save was an agreed requirement, and close the reports as working as designed.
options.rationale: The error is being right about the specification and wrong about the customer. Forty-one reports say a working practice has been removed, and closing them tells the clerks their experience is not evidence.

options.text: Find out what clerks actually did with a half-finished entry, then decide whether the need or the old mechanism is the thing to satisfy.
options.rationale: It separates the underlying need from the habit that served it, which is the only way to tell a genuine gap from nostalgia. Whichever way it resolves, you can explain the decision to the clerks in terms of their own work.

options.text: Escalate to the customer's compliance manager to confirm in writing that validation on save is mandatory.
options.rationale: The error is collecting authority to overrule rather than understanding to decide. A ruling may end the reports, but it leaves forty-one people working around a system they have been told they are wrong about.

questions.explanation: When users describe a replacement system as broken, they are usually describing an expectation formed by the system it replaces, and the question worth asking is what the old behaviour was for. Sometimes it served a real need the new design missed and sometimes it served a workaround that no longer applies, but the two look identical in a defect report. Deciding without asking gets it right by luck.
questions.mindset: Ask what a familiar behaviour was used for before deciding whether losing it is a defect or a change.

questions.stem: You are three months into installing a trade counter and yard stock system for a builders' timber merchant, and three separate customer behaviours have caught your attention this fortnight. Each one is telling you something about an expectation, and each needs a different first response. Match each behaviour to the response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The yard manager has raised the same minor labelling issue at three consecutive progress meetings and has accepted your answer each time.
The finance director, who signs the acceptance certificate, has not attended a review since the kickoff and sends no deputy.
The trade counter supervisor sends detailed written comments after every demonstration, unprompted, and has done so for eleven weeks.

options.text: Ask him what the labelling issue stands for, because something raised three times after being answered is rarely about itself.
options.rationale: Repetition after a satisfactory answer is the signal, not the topic. Treating the fourth raising as a fourth answer misses that he is using a safe subject to keep a larger unease on the agenda.

options.text: Go to her directly and establish what she will be judging when the certificate reaches her.
options.rationale: Absence from a forum is not absence of expectations, and hers are the ones that decide acceptance. Meeting her on her own terms costs an hour and removes the largest unknown on the project.

options.text: Tell her what happened to each of her last three sets of comments, so the effort visibly continues to be worth making.
options.rationale: Unprompted effort is a resource with a short half-life. Closing the loop is what keeps a volunteer channel open, and the fastest way to lose your best source is to let it look like nothing happens.

options.text: Reduce the frequency of progress meetings so that attendance and preparation improve.
options.rationale: Not used. Meeting frequency is not the problem in any of the three: one person attends and repeats himself, one never attends, and one engages outside the meeting entirely. Fewer meetings changes none of that.

questions.explanation: Customer behaviour carries information that customer statements do not, and each characteristic pattern points at a different response: repetition after resolution points at an unspoken concern, absence from the forum points at an unmet person, and sustained unprompted effort points at a channel that needs feeding. The common error is to read all three as engagement problems and apply one remedy, usually a meeting.
questions.mindset: Read how a customer behaves as evidence about expectations, not merely as a comment on your meetings.

questions.stem: Your team builds a picking and grading app for a glasshouse tomato grower. You learn that the head of the packhouse has told her seasonal recruitment agency that the app will halve the time it takes to train a new picker, a claim your team has never made or estimated. She is recruiting 120 seasonal staff in three weeks and has shortened her training programme accordingly. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Go to her now, establish what she needs the app to do for training, and tell her plainly what it will and will not do while she can still change the programme.
options.rationale: The value of acting today is entirely in her decision window, which closes when recruitment starts. It also reframes the conversation around the need behind the claim rather than the accuracy of the claim.

options.text: Correct the claim at the next review so that the record shows what the team has actually committed to.
options.rationale: The error is prioritising the record over the decision. Being able to show you corrected it is worth little once 120 people have been recruited against a training plan that does not work.

options.text: Take no action, since the claim was made by the customer about her own operation and was not a project commitment.
options.rationale: The error is treating the source of an expectation as determining whether you own it. You will be judged against the shortened training programme regardless of who invented it.

options.text: Add halving training time to the next sprint goal so the team is working towards what the customer now expects.
options.rationale: The error is absorbing somebody else's promise into a commitment before knowing whether it can be met. It converts a claim you can still correct into a target you have now adopted.

questions.explanation: Expectations formed inside the customer's organisation are as binding on your project as the ones formed in your own reviews, because the person holding them will act on them. The response that helps is neither to accept the claim nor to disown it, but to reach the person while the decision it feeds is still open. Timing is the whole of the value here: the same conversation a fortnight later is a post-mortem.
questions.mindset: An expectation you did not create is still one you will be measured against, so reach it while the decisions built on it can still move.

questions.stem: For eight months your team has produced an ad-hoc data extract for the quality manager at an aerospace component overhaul customer, roughly a day of effort each month and never part of the agreed scope. You have just seen the customer's revised departmental procedure, effective next quarter, which cites the monthly extract as a control step and names your team as the provider. Nobody has discussed this with you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue producing the extract, since it is a modest effort and the relationship benefits from the goodwill.
options.rationale: The error is letting repeated goodwill mature into an unfunded standing commitment. A day a month that nobody has agreed is a day a month you cannot plan around and cannot stop without a dispute.

options.text: Raise it explicitly with the quality manager and his sponsor, and decide together whether it becomes agreed scope, becomes automated, or ends with notice.
options.rationale: It names the situation before the procedure takes effect and puts the three real options on the table. Deciding it as a service question is what stops it being settled later as an accusation.

options.text: Stop providing the extract and point to the agreed scope, which has never included it.
options.rationale: The error is treating contractual entitlement as the whole question. The customer has built a control step around this, so withdrawing it is a change to their operation whether or not you ever owed it.

options.text: Raise a change request covering the eight months already provided so the effort is recognised and recovered.
options.rationale: The error is monetising work you chose to give away, retrospectively. It reads as an invoice for goodwill and it does not answer the question of what happens next quarter.

questions.explanation: Favours repeated on a schedule stop being favours, and the moment they appear in the customer's own procedures they have become a service level nobody negotiated. The work is to convert the informal arrangement into a decision while there is still no accusation attached, which means naming it early and offering the genuine options rather than either quietly continuing or abruptly stopping. Withdrawing a service is a change to the customer even when it was never in scope.
questions.mindset: Notice when goodwill has hardened into expectation, and put it back on the table before someone else does.

questions.stem: Your customer, a cinema chain, judges the new booking system on a satisfaction survey sent each month to the duty manager at all 48 sites. Last month 12 duty managers responded: 9 rated the system satisfactory or better and 3 did not. Your account team reported customer satisfaction of 75 per cent to the steering group and said the 80 per cent target was nearly met. Work through the figures below.

blanks.label: Response rate, as a percentage of sites surveyed
blanks.rationale: Twelve responses from 48 sites is a quarter of the population. Three sites in four expressed no view at all, which is the fact the headline percentage does not carry.

blanks.label: Percentage of all 48 sites known to be satisfied, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: Nine known-satisfied sites out of 48 is 18.75 per cent. The 75 per cent figure is true only of the twelve who answered, and the two numbers answer different questions.

blanks.label: The property of the sample that the reported 75 per cent conceals
blanks.rationale: A percentage with no denominator attached hides how many people it represents. Reporting the ratio without the response rate lets twelve opinions stand in for a chain of 48.

questions.explanation: A satisfaction figure is a measurement instrument and inherits every weakness of the sample it was drawn from, so the number is only interpretable alongside who answered and who did not. Low response is itself a signal and usually not a neutral one, because the indifferent and the resigned answer least. The discipline is to report the denominator beside the ratio every time, so that a governance body is deciding on evidence rather than on arithmetic.
questions.mindset: Report the denominator with the percentage, because a satisfaction score without its sample is a claim rather than a measurement.

questions.stem: The operations manager of a garden centre group asked for a written weekly status note on the click-and-collect product, and you have sent one every Friday for eleven weeks. In today's review she asks when the collection-slot changes will reach the Cheshire site, which your note has answered in the same paragraph three weeks running. She is not being difficult and plainly has not read them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask her what decisions she needs the weekly note to support, and change its form to serve those.
options.rationale: It treats her not reading as information about the note rather than about her. A report that answers a question she has to ask anyway is not doing the job she asked it to do.

options.text: Resend the last three notes with the relevant paragraph highlighted.
options.rationale: The error is answering an unmet information need through the channel that already failed. It also carries a mild reproach, which is a poor use of the one moment she has shown you what she actually wanted to know.

options.text: Stop producing the weekly note, since eleven weeks of evidence show it is not being used.
options.rationale: The error is withdrawing something the customer asked for without agreeing what replaces it. She wanted the reassurance the note represents, even if the format is wrong.

options.text: Raise with her sponsor that the customer is not engaging with project reporting.
options.rationale: The error is making the customer's inattention a fault to be reported rather than a signal to be acted on. It escalates a problem you could solve with one question.

questions.explanation: A customer's request for a report is a rough statement of an information need, and the format they name is a guess at how to meet it. When the report is not being read, the need has not gone away, so the useful move is to go back to the decision it was meant to support and design from there. Reports are worth what the reader does with them, which is why volume is never evidence of communication.
questions.mindset: Design what you send a customer around the decision it supports, not around the format they first asked for.

questions.stem: At the start of your iron foundry systems project, the melting shop supervisor asked to be involved in any decision that changes how the shop floor works. Last week, under time pressure, you chose the furnace scheduling logic with the customer's IT lead alone. The choice is sound, the supervisor agrees it is the right one technically, and he is angrier than you have seen him. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out the technical reasoning again, since he accepts the decision is correct and the objection should fall away.
options.rationale: The error is answering a complaint about process with an argument about outcome. Repeating why the decision was right tells him the thing he has already conceded and none of the thing he raised.

options.text: Acknowledge that the agreed involvement was missed, and re-agree with him which decisions he is part of before the next one arises.
options.rationale: It responds to what was actually broken, and the forward half matters more than the apology because a vague promise to involve him will fail again under the same pressure. Naming the class of decision is what makes it hold.

options.text: Reverse the scheduling decision and re-take it with him present, so the process is visibly restored.
options.rationale: The error is buying back trust with a technical concession. Undoing a decision both of you think is right teaches him that displeasure moves the project, and invites its use next time.

options.text: Route future shop floor decisions through the customer's sponsor, who can represent operational interests formally.
options.rationale: The error is escalating around the person whose expectation you missed. Replacing him with his senior answers the inconvenience of consulting him and confirms his suspicion that he does not count.

questions.explanation: Customers hold expectations about how they will be treated as well as about what they will receive, and the two fail independently: a project can deliver the right answer and still breach an agreement about who takes part. Process expectations are usually invisible until broken, which is why the ones that are stated out loud deserve a place in the plan. Repairing one means addressing the process, not re-arguing the outcome or trading a concession for the feeling.
questions.mindset: When someone objects to how a decision was taken, do not answer them with why it was right.

questions.stem: Your enrolment product was piloted with one language school, and over four months your team tailored heavily to that school's way of working: bespoke fee bands, its own placement test flow, its own reporting. You are now rolling out to nine further schools in the same group. Two of them have already asked, in writing, for the placement test flow they have heard the pilot school has. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish which of the pilot's tailored behaviours the other nine actually need before deciding what becomes standard product.
options.rationale: It tests whether the request is a genuine need or an echo of hearing that someone else has something. What one customer needed under close attention is a hypothesis about the group, not a finding.

options.text: Tell the pilot school which of its tailored behaviours will not survive the roll-out, and when they will change.
options.rationale: The pilot school has built working practice on capability that was always provisional, and notice is what turns a loss into a plan. Saying nothing leaves them discovering it on the day it disappears.

options.text: Make all of the pilot tailoring standard, so that no school feels it has been given a lesser product.
options.rationale: The error is letting one customer's expectations define the product for ten. Tailoring earned by four months of close attention becomes permanent complexity that the other nine will pay for in every future change.

options.text: Strip out all tailoring at roll-out and treat the pilot build as a throwaway prototype.
options.rationale: The error is withdrawing capability the pilot customer now depends on, without notice, as an internal tidying decision. It also discards findings that were expensive to get.

options.text: Let each of the nine schools request its own tailoring during roll-out, on the same basis the pilot did.
options.rationale: The error is treating expectation-gathering as order-taking. Ten variants means ten products, and expectations then move faster across the group than any team can meet them.

questions.explanation: A pilot generates two things that are easily confused: evidence about what customers need, and a set of expectations held by the pilot customer and by everyone who has heard about it. Scaling means deciding which of the tailoring was a finding and which was a courtesy, and being explicit with the pilot about what it is losing. The failure mode at either extreme is the same, which is letting one customer's experience settle a question that belongs to all of them.
questions.mindset: Treat what a pilot customer received as a hypothesis about the rest, not as a promise already made to them.

questions.stem: A self-storage operator has commissioned a new site management system. The finance director signed the order and has been clear about what he wants: card payment reconciliation that closes in one pass. Six weeks in, you realise nobody has spoken to the site assistants who will use the system for eight hours a day, and the finance director has not suggested it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Build to the finance director's stated expectations, since he commissioned the work and controls the budget.
options.rationale: The error is treating budget authority as the whole of the customer. He can tell you what he will pay for and not whether the assistants can work the system, and adoption is decided by people who never signed anything.

options.text: Propose to the finance director that you spend time with the site assistants, and bring what you learn back through him.
options.rationale: It opens the missing source of expectations while keeping the paying customer in the loop rather than around him. Going through him also gets his read on what the assistants say, which is information you need.

options.text: Interview the site assistants and add their needs to the backlog directly, keeping the finance director's items at the top.
options.rationale: The error is creating a second expectation channel the paying customer does not know exists. It works until the first conflict, at which point he discovers he has been committing to things he never saw.

options.text: Ask the finance director to nominate a site assistant to represent the others, and take that person's view as the user position.
options.rationale: The error is delegating the discovery rather than doing it. A nominee chosen by the signatory gives you one person's account, filtered by who was comfortable to put forward.

questions.explanation: The person who buys and the people who use are routinely different, and their expectations fail in different ways: the buyer's are stated and the users' are assumed. Reaching the users is necessary, but doing it around the buyer trades one gap for a worse one, because it leaves the person accountable for the money unaware of what is shaping the work. The route matters as much as the discovery.
questions.mindset: Go to the users for expectations the buyer cannot hold, and go through the buyer to get there.

questions.stem: Your traceability system for a shellfish purification plant was expected to give provenance to the individual harvesting bed. Six weeks ago you established that the harvest data the plant receives from its own gatherers is only ever accurate to a bay, which no software of yours can improve. You have not yet said so. Last week the plant used bed-level traceability as a differentiator in a tender for a supermarket contract. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell the plant director now, with the evidence and the options, even though the tender has already been submitted.
options.rationale: The tender being gone does not close every decision: there is still the clarification stage, the contract terms and how the plant prepares its gatherers. Telling him today is what puts those decisions back in his hands.

options.text: Deliver bay-level traceability as designed and explain the limitation at handover, when the system can be demonstrated.
options.rationale: The error is letting a known unmet expectation run until it can only be received as a failure. A limitation disclosed at handover has stopped being a decision and become an accusation.

options.text: Work with the gatherers to improve the accuracy of harvest records before raising the limitation with the customer.
options.rationale: The error is making the customer's commercial exposure wait on a third party you do not control. The work may be worth doing, but doing it first means he is uninformed for however long it takes.

options.text: Record it in the risk register and raise it formally at the steering group in three weeks.
options.rationale: The error is using the right instrument on the wrong clock. The register is where a project remembers things; it is not a way of telling the one person whose commercial decisions depend on knowing.

options.text: Offer a manual reconciliation step at go-live so bed-level reporting is possible, without stating that the data limitation is permanent.
options.rationale: The error is dressing a permanent constraint as a temporary inconvenience. A workaround presented without its ceiling leaves the customer still believing the capability is coming.

questions.explanation: Bad news about what a customer will not get has a value that decays hourly, because its only use is in the decisions still open when it arrives. The instinct to wait for a better moment, a fuller answer or a formal forum reliably costs the customer options, and it converts a constraint that could have been managed into a broken promise. Holding a known limitation past the point of usefulness is a choice, however it is filed.
questions.mindset: Deliver news of what cannot be done while it can still change what someone decides.

questions.stem: Your project delivers a stock export for a customer's warehouse, and in the space of one week three different things have been said about whether supplier codes appear in that export. They came from different people with different standing, and treating them alike would be a mistake. Complete each sentence with the classification that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The site manager says he would quite like supplier codes included and would not delay go-live for them. This is best handled as
The signed specification states the export must carry supplier codes and makes acceptance conditional on it. This is best handled as
The customer's external auditors have never mentioned supplier codes, but will refuse the annual stock audit without them. This is best handled as

options.text: a preference, recorded and offered whenever including it happens to be cheap
options.rationale: He has attached no consequence to going without, which is what separates a preference from a requirement. Recording it still matters, because preferences are how you spend small amounts of goodwill well.

options.text: a requirement, verified at acceptance against the agreed criteria
options.rationale: It is written, agreed and carries a stated consequence for acceptance. This is the only one of the three where the test is already defined and the answer is already settled.

options.text: an unstated expectation, confirmed with the auditors before it can become a failure
options.rationale: Nobody has said it, everybody assumes it, and it will be discovered at the audit if not before. Unstated expectations held by third parties are the ones that surface as crises.

options.text: a change request raised against the current baseline
options.rationale: Not used. A change request applies where an agreed baseline is being altered. None of the three is that: one is a wish, one is already in the baseline, and one has never been captured at all.

questions.explanation: Things a customer says about what they want are not equivalent, and the useful distinction is what happens if the thing does not appear. A preference has no consequence attached, a requirement has an agreed test, and an unstated expectation has a real consequence and no test at all, which makes it the most dangerous of the three. Sorting them on arrival is what stops a project treating wishes as commitments while assumptions go unexamined.
questions.mindset: Sort what a customer says by what happens if it is missing, not by how firmly it was said.

questions.stem: For two months the growing manager at a mushroom farm criticised your yield tracking product at every fortnightly review: too many taps, wrong units, reports he cannot use. Then the complaints stopped. He has now missed the last three reviews, sending no deputy and no comment. Your delivery has not changed in any way that would account for it, and your account lead is treating the quiet as progress. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Go to him directly and find out why he has stopped attending, treating the silence as the signal.
options.rationale: Someone who complained for two months and then stopped has either been satisfied or given up, and only one of those is good news. The distinction cannot be made from a distance and cannot wait.

options.text: Report the drop in complaints as improving customer satisfaction and continue to the next increment.
options.rationale: The error is reading silence as consent. Complaints are a form of engagement, and their disappearance without a corresponding change in the product is the least reassuring version of quiet.

options.text: Ask the farm to appoint a more available representative to the reviews so attendance is reliable.
options.rationale: The error is treating an engagement signal as a diary problem and solving it by replacing the person. It removes the symptom and the only witness to the cause.

options.text: Send him a short satisfaction survey so his current view is captured in a form you can track.
options.rationale: The error is reaching for an instrument that returns a score instead of a reason, aimed at someone who has already stopped spending effort on you. Low-effort channels fail hardest with disengaged people.

questions.explanation: A customer who stops complaining has either been satisfied or has concluded that complaining does not work, and the two look identical in any metric built on volume of feedback. Because disengagement is quiet and satisfaction is quiet, silence must be investigated rather than interpreted. The general form is that any improvement in a measure that you cannot trace to a change you made deserves more suspicion than the problem it appears to have solved.
questions.mindset: Treat a customer going quiet as a question to investigate, never as an answer you have been given.

questions.stem: Requirements for a probate service's case management replacement were agreed with the head of registry fourteen months ago. Procurement then stalled and has only now completed. At your restart meeting she tells you, warmly and without hesitation, that nothing has changed and you should carry on from where the team left off. Two of her four team leaders are new and case volumes are up by a third. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the assurance and restart against the agreed requirements, since she is best placed to know what has changed in her own service.
options.rationale: The error is taking a general assurance as an answer to a specific list. She is answering a question about her intentions, not auditing forty requirements against fourteen months of operational change.

options.text: Test the assurance against what has demonstrably moved, then re-confirm the requirements item by item with her and the new team leaders.
options.rationale: It uses the evidence you already hold, new staff and a third more volume, to make the review concrete rather than sceptical. Confirming line by line is also how the new team leaders inherit the agreement.

options.text: Re-run requirements elicitation from the beginning, since a fourteen-month gap makes the earlier work unreliable.
options.rationale: The error is paying full price to rediscover things that genuinely have not moved. It also tells a customer who invested weeks in the original work that you consider it wasted.

options.text: Restart as agreed and handle any drift through change control as it surfaces during delivery.
options.rationale: The error is electing to discover drift at the most expensive moment. Change control is designed for changes that arise, not as a mechanism for finding out what was already stale on day one.

questions.explanation: Agreed expectations decay with time, staff turnover and volume change, and a customer's assurance that nothing has changed is usually sincere and usually wrong, because nobody re-reads a list before answering. The proportionate response is neither acceptance nor a fresh start but a targeted re-confirmation aimed at what you can show has moved. A pause in a project is a period during which the customer kept operating.
questions.mindset: After any long gap, re-confirm expectations against what has demonstrably changed rather than against how confidently you are reassured.

questions.stem: A credit union with nine branches is replacing its member records platform. Each branch manager has views, they conflict on how member identity checks should work, and none has authority over another. Head office employs four people and says it will support whatever the branches decide. You have three weeks of discovery. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree with the chief executive a single named person with authority to settle disagreements between branches.
options.rationale: Nine equal voices with no tiebreak produces either paralysis or whichever expectation was expressed most forcefully. Someone must be able to decide, and the time to name them is before the first deadlock.

options.text: Sample branches deliberately for discovery, choosing the largest, the smallest and the most operationally unusual.
options.rationale: Deliberate sampling covers the range of ways the platform will be used, which nine identical conversations would not. It also spends three weeks where the differences actually are.

options.text: Run a workshop with all nine managers and record whatever consensus emerges as the customer position.
options.rationale: The error is mistaking a meeting outcome for a mandate. Consensus in a room rewards whoever argues longest and produces a position nobody has authority to hold to afterwards.

options.text: Take head office's stated view as the customer position, since it exists to represent all nine branches.
options.rationale: The error is assuming representation without testing it. Head office has already said it will follow the branches, so treating it as the voice of the customer manufactures an answer out of a deferral.

options.text: Collect every branch's requirements and build the union of them, so that no branch is left unserved.
options.rationale: The error is treating expectation-gathering as accumulation. Conflicting identity check rules cannot all be built, and a union of nine wish lists hides the conflicts rather than resolving them.

questions.explanation: Where a customer is a federation rather than a person, two things have to be established before requirements mean anything: who can decide when parts of the customer disagree, and how the range of the customer will be sampled given that you cannot talk to all of it. Neither is a requirements question, and skipping them produces a plan built on whichever voice was loudest in the room.
questions.mindset: When the customer is many people, settle who decides and who you will listen to before asking what they want.

questions.stem: You are delivering a new production and cataloguing system for a sight-loss charity's talking books service. Your own organisation's fundraising team has sent an appeal to 40,000 supporters saying the system will double the number of titles produced each year. Your team has never estimated any such figure. The service manager has begun telling volunteer narrators about the increase, and the next appeal goes out in a month. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Adopt doubling annual titles as a project objective, since it is now the public commitment of the organisation.
options.rationale: The error is accepting a number invented outside the project as a target inside it. Committing to a figure nobody derived means the first honest forecast becomes a failure report.

options.text: Go to the fundraising owner to establish what the project can defensibly claim, and separately tell the service manager what the system will and will not change.
options.rationale: It corrects the claim at its source before the next appeal and reaches the person already acting on it. Both halves are needed, because fixing the message does not unwind what the narrators have been told.

options.text: Leave it, since fundraising material is not a project artefact and carries no delivery commitment.
options.rationale: The error is deciding ownership of an expectation by where it originated. Volunteers and supporters do not distinguish between the charity's appeal and the project's promise, and neither will the review afterwards.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct fundraising to withdraw the claim and issue a correction to supporters.
options.rationale: The error is escalating to compel before establishing the facts. It turns a colleague with a correctable draft into an opponent defending a published position, and a public retraction may harm the charity more than the claim did.

questions.explanation: Expectations are set by whoever speaks to the audience, and a project frequently finds itself accountable for claims made by its own marketing, its sponsor or its sales team. The response has two parts that are easy to confuse: correcting the claim at its source, which protects future audiences, and reaching the people already acting on it, which protects the present. Escalation is a poor substitute for either, because it settles who is at fault rather than what people now believe.
questions.mindset: Correct an over-claim at its source and reach the people already planning around it, because doing only one leaves the expectation in place.

questions.stem: A vineyard group has asked that all requests, defects and priorities for your harvest logistics product be tracked in their own workflow tool, which your team does not use and finds slow. Your team already runs a board that works well. The customer's programme lead has raised this twice and is now insistent, saying she cannot see what is happening. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what she needs her tool to give her, then meet that need from one system of record, mirroring deliberately if that is what it takes.
options.rationale: Her stated request is a tool; her stated reason is visibility. Solving the reason keeps a single authoritative record, which is the property that actually protects both sides.

options.text: Adopt the customer's tool for all project tracking, since accommodating how the customer works is part of the service.
options.rationale: The error is taking on a change to your team's working practice to satisfy a need you have not identified. If she wanted a weekly view, you have paid for it with everything the team's board was doing.

options.text: Decline and offer her read-only access to the team's board instead.
options.rationale: The error is answering a stated need with your own convenience. Access to an unfamiliar board that uses your team's shorthand is not the same as visibility, and she has already said twice that she cannot see what is happening.

options.text: Maintain both systems fully, so the team keeps its board and the customer gets everything in hers.
options.rationale: The error is accepting two systems of record. They will disagree within weeks, and the moment they do, both become things the customer cannot trust.

questions.explanation: A request to work in the customer's tooling is nearly always a request for visibility wearing the clothes of a request for a tool, and the two have quite different solutions. Establishing the underlying need lets you satisfy it while preserving the property that matters most, which is that exactly one record is authoritative. Duplicate records are worse than an inconvenient single one, because divergence destroys trust in both.
questions.mindset: Find the need behind a request for your team to work differently, and keep one record authoritative whatever you agree.

questions.stem: The chart tracks your housekeeping system rollout for a hotel group over eight months. The upper line is cumulative functionality accepted by the customer; the lower line is the monthly satisfaction score returned by the group's operations team. Your account review last week concluded that the relationship deteriorated in month six. Select the point at which the customer's expectations first diverged from what delivery was giving them.

graphic.title: Accepted functionality and customer satisfaction plotted monthly over eight months
graphic.caption: Select a point on the chart. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between points, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Month 2 — both lines rising together
regions.rationale: Both measures are moving the same way here, which is the pattern you want rather than a warning. Choosing it mistakes the first visible movement on the chart for the first meaningful one.

regions.label: Month 4 — accepted functionality still rising, satisfaction flat
regions.rationale: Divergence begins where the two lines stop moving together, not where they cross or where one falls. From here you are delivering more and being credited with nothing, which is the earliest point action was possible.

regions.label: Month 6 — satisfaction begins to fall
regions.rationale: This is where the problem becomes obvious, two months after it became visible. Reading the decline as the start is what produced the account review's conclusion and cost the project its warning period.

regions.label: Month 8 — satisfaction falls below its month-one level
regions.rationale: Waiting for a score to breach its starting level is waiting for a threshold rather than watching a trend. By this point the customer has been unhappy for four months.

questions.explanation: Satisfaction data is only useful as an early warning if it is read against what was delivered over the same period, because the signal is the relationship between the two lines rather than the level of either. A flat score during a period of heavy delivery says expectations are moving away from what is being built, and it says so months before the score falls. Waiting for a decline converts a leading indicator into a lagging one.
questions.mindset: Read a satisfaction trend against what was delivered beside it, and treat the loss of correlation as the warning.

questions.stem: A dry cleaning chain is replacing the till and garment tracking system across 60 shops. At the planning workshop the managing director says, several times and with feeling, that the system must work perfectly from day one because his customers do not forgive lost garments. He will not be drawn on what perfectly means. Go-live is in four months. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with him in advance which classes of defect would stop go-live and which would be accepted with a committed fix date.
options.rationale: It converts an absolute nobody can verify into a rule you can both apply on the day. Doing it now also lets him express what he actually fears, which is losing garments rather than every possible fault.

options.text: Reassure him that the test approach is thorough and describe the coverage the team will achieve.
options.rationale: The error is answering an expectation with confidence instead of a criterion. He will accept the reassurance and keep the original standard, so nothing has been agreed and the argument simply moves to go-live weekend.

options.text: Accept zero defects as the standard, since the customer is entitled to set the quality bar he is paying for.
options.rationale: The error is agreeing to a standard that cannot be verified or met. An unachievable commitment guarantees a dispute on the day, and it will be argued from a position you accepted in writing.

options.text: Explain that all systems of this size ship with known defects and that zero is not a realistic target.
options.rationale: The error is correcting the customer about the industry rather than finding out what he is protecting. It is true, it sounds like preparation for excuses, and it leaves his real concern unexamined.

questions.explanation: A customer's quality expectation usually arrives as an absolute because absolutes are how people express fear, and the useful move is to trade the absolute for a decision rule while the conversation is still hypothetical. Agreeing what would and would not stop a go-live does two jobs: it makes the standard testable, and it surfaces which failures the customer genuinely cannot tolerate. Both are far cheaper to establish before the date than during it.
questions.mindset: Turn an absolute quality expectation into an agreed decision rule while it is still hypothetical.

questions.stem: Your product serves a cold-store haulier, and three of the customer's expectations have moved this quarter for quite different reasons. Handling all three the same way would be an expensive habit, because each one is asking for a different mechanism. Match each situation to the response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The operations director wants delivery-window planning two quarters earlier than the roadmap shows, and has named the feature she would give up to get it.
The customer's expectation of how fast your team responds to production incidents has drifted from next working day to within the hour, with nothing agreed or discussed.
A feature you delivered and they accepted last quarter no longer does what they need, because their contract with a supermarket changed the temperature reporting they must provide.

options.text: Re-prioritise the backlog with her, taking up the trade she has already offered.
options.rationale: She has moved a priority and named the cost she will pay, which is exactly the input prioritisation exists to consume. Treating a well-formed trade as a problem teaches customers to stop offering them.

options.text: Reopen the service agreement explicitly, because a response level that has drifted is one nobody has agreed to resource.
options.rationale: Drift in a service expectation is invisible until it is missed, and by then it has the standing of a promise. Making it explicit forces the question of what the faster level would cost and who is paying.

options.text: Treat it as new work in a changed context rather than as a defect in what was accepted.
options.rationale: The delivered feature still meets the criteria it was accepted against; what changed is outside it. Classing it as a defect would make your team liable for the customer's commercial changes without limit.

options.text: Log it in the risk register and monitor whether the situation recurs.
options.rationale: Not used. Monitoring is what you do when the cause is unknown and the effect is uncertain. All three of these have a known cause and a decision waiting, so logging any of them would simply defer it.

questions.explanation: Expectations move for different reasons and each reason has its own proper mechanism: a re-prioritisation for a changed priority, a renegotiated service level for a drifting service, and new work for a changed external context. Applying one mechanism to all three is the common failure, and it is usually the risk register, because filing something feels like handling it. Classification is what decides whether the response can work at all.
questions.mindset: Match the mechanism to why the expectation moved, because the wrong instrument records a decision instead of taking it.

questions.stem: At a trade show last week your organisation's sales lead told the technical director of an anaerobic digestion operator that the control dashboard you are building will show gas yield per feedstock batch. It is not in the agreed scope. It is feasible but would take most of a release. The technical director has since referenced it in an email about their feedstock trial planning. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Get the sales lead, yourself and the technical director into one conversation quickly, establish what was said and heard, and re-set the position before the trial planning hardens.
options.rationale: It settles the internal disagreement and the customer's understanding in the same conversation, which is the only way neither is left holding a different version. Speed matters because his trial plan is being written now.

options.text: Build the capability, on the basis that a commitment made by your organisation is a commitment the project honours.
options.rationale: The error is treating every informal statement as binding, which makes scope a function of who spoke to the customer most recently. Most of a release is being spent without anyone deciding it is the best use of it.

options.text: Tell the technical director it was never in scope and refer him to the agreed specification.
options.rationale: The error is putting the customer inside your organisation's internal disagreement. It is contractually correct and it asks him to work out which of two people from your company to believe.

options.text: Ask the sales lead to go back and retract the statement himself, since he made it.
options.rationale: The error is leaving the correction with the person least motivated to make it and least able to explain the delivery position. Ownership of the mistake is not the same as ownership of the fix.

questions.explanation: Expectations set by colleagues outside the delivery team are not the customer's fault and cannot be corrected by pointing at the contract, because the customer heard one organisation speak. The response that works is a single conversation containing everyone who holds a version, held quickly, before the customer has built plans that make retreat expensive. Correcting through intermediaries reliably produces a third version.
questions.mindset: When your own organisation has set an expectation you cannot meet, correct it in one conversation that includes everyone who holds a version.

questions.stem: Your support agreement with a coach tour operator promises a response within four working hours, where the working day is defined in an annexe as 09:00 to 17:00, Monday to Friday. The operator's duty manager has told his team you will always come back within four hours, and he runs tours seven days a week. An incident is raised at 16:00 on a Friday. Work through the figures below.

blanks.label: Elapsed calendar hours from the incident to the contractual response deadline
blanks.rationale: One working hour remains on Friday, taking the clock to 17:00, and the remaining three fall between 09:00 and 12:00 on Monday. From 16:00 Friday to 12:00 Monday is 68 elapsed hours.

blanks.label: Elapsed calendar hours the duty manager believes he is entitled to
blanks.rationale: He has understood four hours as four hours, which puts his expected response at 20:00 on the Friday evening. Nothing in what he was told signals that a clock stops overnight or at weekends.

blanks.label: The size of the expectation gap, in hours
blanks.rationale: Sixty-eight hours against four leaves a gap of 64 hours, almost three days. The gap is invisible until an incident falls at the wrong end of a week, which is when it does the most damage.

blanks.label: The term in the agreement that produces the difference
blanks.rationale: The word working carries the entire difference between the two numbers, and it is defined in an annexe rather than in the clause the customer reads.

questions.explanation: A service level is a definition as much as a number, and the qualifiers that scope it are usually held somewhere the customer never reads. Gaps of this kind stay dormant for months and then appear as a breach at the least convenient moment, which is why the worked example, rather than the clause, is what should be walked through with the customer at the start. Any commitment with a clock attached should be tested against the customer's worst realistic timing before it is signed.
questions.mindset: Walk a service commitment through its worst timing with the customer, because the qualifiers are where expectations quietly separate.

questions.stem: Your test-requesting product serves two groups within the same pathology customer. General practices want fewer clicks and default test panels. Hospital consultants argue that default panels drive over-testing and want granular selection with no defaults. Both are right about their own work. Your product owner, who reports to the laboratory director, has asked your team to decide the design and get on with it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Make the divergence explicit with the trade named, and take it to someone with authority over both groups to decide.
options.rationale: The conflict is between two legitimate customer positions with a clinical and financial trade behind it, which is a governance decision rather than a design one. Naming the trade is what makes it decidable rather than a matter of taste.

options.text: Implement both behaviours behind a role-based setting so each group gets what it expects.
options.rationale: The error is answering an unresolved conflict of expectations with permanent product complexity. The disagreement does not go away; it returns at every subsequent change, now with two code paths to maintain.

options.text: Follow the general practices, since they generate the great majority of requests and the volume benefit is larger.
options.rationale: The error is settling a conflict by counting when the objection is about clinical harm. Volume is a real consideration, but it does not answer an argument about over-testing.

options.text: Follow the consultants, since a clinical risk argument outweighs a convenience argument.
options.rationale: The error is the team adopting a clinical position that belongs to the customer's governance. The reasoning may be sound, and it is still your team deciding something nobody authorised you to decide.

questions.explanation: When two parts of one customer hold expectations that cannot both be met, the delivery team's job is to make the conflict visible and decidable, not to resolve it. Building both is the most tempting evasion because it looks like service, while in fact it defers the decision into the product where it becomes permanent. Escalation here is not a failure of initiative; it is routing a decision to the only place it can legitimately be made.
questions.mindset: Where two customers want incompatible things, your job is to name the trade and route the decision, not to pick a side.

questions.stem: An electoral services team is the customer for a new register and postal vote system that must run for a statutory poll in May. Asked to resource user acceptance testing, the electoral services manager says you built it, so you should test it, and that her four staff have no hours to spare before the canvass. The date cannot move. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish what she is actually short of — hours, confidence about what to test, or skills — and shape the testing around that constraint.
options.rationale: Refusal to test is usually a capacity or confidence problem wearing the language of principle. Which one it is decides whether the answer is a shorter script, a facilitated session or borrowed staff.

options.text: State in writing to her and the sponsor what accepting without customer testing means for who owns fitness for purpose in May.
options.rationale: It makes an implicit transfer of judgement visible while there is still time to change it. This is not defensive paperwork: it is the fact most likely to release the four hours she says she does not have.

options.text: Have your own team test on her behalf and present the results to her as the basis for acceptance.
options.rationale: The error is signing the customer's judgement in her name. Your team can prove the system does what was specified and cannot decide whether it works for an election office under canvass pressure.

options.text: Escalate to the returning officer to require her staff to attend testing sessions.
options.rationale: The error is compelling participation, which produces attendance rather than judgement. People sent to test under instruction sign the form and tell you nothing you needed to know.

options.text: Delay go-live until the customer commits testing resource, since acceptance cannot be meaningful without it.
options.rationale: The error is answering a capacity problem with a schedule penalty against a statutory date. The poll happens in May whether or not the system is ready, so delay removes options without adding any.

questions.explanation: Acceptance testing is where a customer converts their expectations into a judgement, and it cannot be performed for them however good the coverage. When the customer will not or cannot take part, the work is to reduce what participation costs them and to make the consequence of not participating explicit and early. Compulsion and delay both look decisive and neither produces the thing that was missing, which is the customer's own opinion.
questions.mindset: Make customer testing cheap for the customer and its absence explicit, because nobody can hold an expectation on their behalf.

questions.stem: You hold a five-year framework with a ski lift operator whose duty managers are seasonal. Each winter a new cohort arrives, having been trained by last season's leavers on the workarounds rather than the system, and each winter they raise the same complaints and expect capabilities that were considered and rejected two seasons ago. Your team finds this demoralising. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Build a short induction to what the system does and does not do, owned jointly with the operator and timed to their recruitment cycle.
options.rationale: Turnover is a permanent feature of this customer rather than an annual accident, so the countermeasure has to be permanent too. Joint ownership matters because an induction the operator does not run will not survive their busy season.

options.text: Treat each arriving cohort as a fresh source of expectations and record what has genuinely changed about how the lifts are run.
options.rationale: Some of what new people raise is ignorance of history and some is a real change in operations that nobody logged. Assuming it is all the former is how a long framework stops noticing its customer.

options.text: Ask the operator to retain duty managers across seasons so there is continuity to work with.
options.rationale: The error is asking the customer to change their staffing model to suit your engagement plan. Seasonal hiring is the business they are in, and the request signals that their reality is an inconvenience.

options.text: Rely on the framework's signed service description to settle the recurring disputes about capability.
options.rationale: The error is expecting a document to do the work of an expectation. It settles entitlement with someone arguing about contract, and it settles nothing with a duty manager in week two of a season.

options.text: Implement the workarounds as product features, so the system behaves the way arriving staff have been taught.
options.rationale: The error is institutionalising accidents of history as requirements. Workarounds encode the gaps of a particular season, and building them makes each year's improvisations permanent.

questions.explanation: On a long engagement the customer is a population rather than a set of people, and it turns over. Expectations therefore have to be re-established as a routine rather than captured once, and each new cohort brings both stale complaints and genuine operational change that arrive looking identical. The two failure modes are treating everything new as noise and treating everything new as requirement, and both are avoided by the same habit of deliberate, scheduled re-listening.
questions.mindset: On a long engagement, plan to re-establish expectations with each new cohort rather than assuming the customer you agreed with is still there.

questions.stem: You message the owner of a beekeeping supplies retailer to say the team plans to change how backorders appear, so that out-of-stock items sit in a separate section of the basket rather than showing an estimated date. Twenty minutes later she replies: yeah, that's fine. The change affects what her customers see at checkout and the team starts on it tomorrow. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Write back setting out what shoppers will see after the change, and ask her to confirm that is what she is agreeing to.
options.rationale: It costs one message and closes the gap between a quick acknowledgement and an informed agreement. Doing it before the work starts means a correction is free rather than rework.

options.text: Proceed with the change, since the customer was asked and has agreed.
options.rationale: The error is taking a casual acknowledgement for informed agreement. Three words sent in twenty minutes is evidence that she read the message, not that she pictured her checkout.

options.text: Send her a change form to sign so the agreement is properly recorded.
options.rationale: The error is reaching for formality out of proportion to the change. It answers the record-keeping question rather than the understanding question, and it slows a small customer down for no gain.

options.text: Raise it at the review in a fortnight, when the change can be demonstrated and properly agreed.
options.rationale: The error is deferring confirmation until after the work has been done. Agreement obtained once something is built is not agreement, because the cost of saying no has changed.

questions.explanation: Agreement obtained in passing is worth roughly what it cost to give, and the fix is not more formality but a short restatement of the consequence in the customer's own terms. The test is whether the customer has been told what they will see and do differently, since that is what they will react to later. Confirming before work starts keeps disagreement cheap, which is the whole reason for asking early.
questions.mindset: Confirm what a quick yes actually commits the customer to, in terms of what they will see.

questions.stem: Your survey data project for a dredging contractor reports against three agreed indicators: survey coverage, report delivery within two days, and data accuracy. All three are green and have been for months. The harbourmaster who commissioned the work tells you at a site visit that nothing has improved, because what he cares about is the time from survey to a dredge decision, and that is unchanged at eleven days. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue reporting against the agreed indicators, since those are the measures the customer signed and the project is meeting them.
options.rationale: The error is treating agreement on a measure as agreement on the outcome. It is how a project comes to be green in every report and regarded as a failure by the person it was built for.

options.text: Bring the survey-to-decision time into reporting alongside the agreed indicators, and take to the sponsor the question of whether the success measures should change.
options.rationale: Measuring what the customer cares about starts immediately and costs nothing; changing what the project is held to is a governance decision. Separating the two lets you act now without re-baselining unilaterally.

options.text: Switch reporting to survey-to-decision time, since that is what the customer actually values.
options.rationale: The error is changing the project's success measures without the people who set them. Your governance is left holding indicators you have stopped reporting, and the change looks like a response to criticism.

options.text: Record the harbourmaster's concern in the risk register as a threat to benefits realisation.
options.rationale: The error is filing a present fact as a future possibility. He is not warning you that dissatisfaction might occur; he is telling you it exists, and the register is where that will now sit undisturbed.

questions.explanation: A project can meet every agreed measure and still fail the customer, because indicators are proxies chosen early and the thing the customer cares about can sit outside all of them. When the two come apart, the honest response is to start measuring the thing that matters while raising, through governance, whether the formal measures should follow. Reporting green against proxies you know the customer disregards is the point at which reporting stops being information.
questions.mindset: When your indicators are green and the customer is not, believe the customer and put the measure they use in front of your governance.

questions.stem: The diagram shows how expectations reach you on a franchise network project: 210 driving school franchisees raise items in a members' forum; six elected representatives meet quarterly and produce a themed list; the franchisor's operations board selects and funds from that list; your steering group instructs you. Franchisee satisfaction is falling while your steering group reports the project on track. Select the point at which the franchisees' expectations are being lost.

graphic.title: Four-stage chain carrying franchisee expectations from members to the project
graphic.caption: Select a stage. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: 210 franchisees — raise items continuously in the members' forum
regions.rationale: Expectations exist here in full and in the words of the people who hold them, so nothing is lost at the source. Selecting it blames the customer for the fidelity of a channel you designed.

regions.label: Six elected representatives — meet quarterly, produce a themed list
regions.rationale: Two hundred and ten voices become six people's themes once a quarter, so this stage compresses and delays in the same step. Anything that does not fit a theme, or arrives in the wrong week, does not exist further up.

regions.label: Operations board — selects and funds items from the themed list
regions.rationale: The board decides between the options it receives and can only be as good as its input. Choosing it mistakes a prioritisation point for a listening failure, and would send you to fix funding rules that are working as intended.

regions.label: Steering group — instructs the project and reports its status
regions.rationale: This is the last relay and it is reporting faithfully what reached it, which is why the status is green. Correcting here improves your reporting and changes nothing about what the franchisees experience.

questions.explanation: Where expectations travel through several hands, the useful question is which stage loses the most and how, and the two mechanisms to look for are compression and delay. A stage that does both at once is nearly always the point of loss, and it is rarely the stage that produced the misleading status, which is why the reporting layer attracts the blame. Shortening or supplementing the lossy stage is the fix; auditing the last relay is not.
questions.mindset: Trace where expectations are compressed and delayed on their way to you, rather than blaming the stage that reported the status.

questions.stem: Your team releases every fortnight to a sleep clinic group. Each release changes something clinic staff see, and every change obliges the clinic to brief 40 technicians and reissue a standard operating procedure, which takes them about six weeks. The clinical services lead has asked you twice to slow down, and your team reads this as the customer not wanting improvements. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep releasing fortnightly but separate release from exposure, agreeing with her when changes become visible to clinic staff.
options.rationale: It solves the constraint she actually has, which is briefing capacity, without giving up the short feedback loop that protects both of you. The decoupling also gives her a predictable date to plan the briefings around.

options.text: Move to a six-week release cadence to match the clinic's ability to absorb change.
options.rationale: The error is slowing delivery to solve an adoption problem. You lose four weeks of feedback on every change, and the clinic's briefing burden per release rises because more has changed at once.

options.text: Continue as you are and support the clinic to keep pace, since frequent small changes are easier to absorb than large ones.
options.rationale: The error is measuring delivery by what leaves your team rather than what the customer can use. Telling a customer their absorption rate is wrong does not raise it.

options.text: Batch six weeks of changes into a single larger release so the clinic briefs once per cycle.
options.rationale: The error is the previous one with more risk attached. It matches her cycle by concentrating change, so each release is harder to brief, harder to test and harder to unpick when something is wrong.

questions.explanation: Delivery pace and adoption pace are different rates constrained by different things, and a customer asking you to slow down is usually describing the second. Decoupling them lets the team keep the feedback loop that makes iterative work worth doing while the customer controls when their people meet the change. Value is only realised at the customer's rate, but that is an argument for scheduling exposure, not for building more slowly.
questions.mindset: Separate how fast you can release from how fast the customer can absorb, and let the customer set the second.

questions.stem: Your team keeps a live list of what a private hire fleet operator expects from the booking and dispatch product. It holds 32 entries. Eighteen were confirmed with the operations director within the last quarter. Nine were captured from meeting notes and have never been put back to the customer. Five were confirmed fourteen months ago and concern a depot the operator closed in the spring. Work through the figures below.

blanks.label: Number of entries you cannot currently claim the operator agrees with
blanks.rationale: The nine never confirmed and the five confirmed against a depot that no longer exists both fail the test. Confirmation that has expired is no better evidence than confirmation never sought.

blanks.label: That number as a percentage of the list, to the nearest whole number
blanks.rationale: Fourteen of 32 is 43.75 per cent, so 44 to the nearest whole number. Close to half the register is being treated as agreed while resting on nothing the customer would recognise.

blanks.label: In one word, what should happen to an entry whose operating context no longer exists
blanks.rationale: An entry about a closed depot cannot be met or tested, so leaving it in place inflates the register and hides how much of it is live. Retiring it is a decision to record, not an admission of error.

questions.explanation: A register of customer expectations is a set of claims with dates attached, and both halves matter: an unconfirmed entry was never the customer's, and a confirmed entry can be overtaken by events in their business. Reviewing for staleness is therefore as important as capturing, and the useful discipline is to hold a confirmation date beside every line so the proportion resting on nothing can be seen at a glance rather than discovered at acceptance.
questions.mindset: Give every recorded expectation a confirmation date, because agreement expires when the customer's circumstances move.

questions.stem: After a site walk at a glass recycling facility, you wrote up what the plant manager expects from the new batch quality reporting: three shift reports a day, a contamination trend by supplier, and an alert when cullet colour mix drifts. Your notes are careful and your monthly report to the sponsor quotes them. The plant manager has never seen any of it written down. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Send him the written expectations and ask him to correct anything you have misheard or that has since moved.
options.rationale: It converts your interpretation into his agreement, and the invitation to correct is what makes replying easy. Asking early also catches the changes he has not thought to mention.

options.text: Rely on the notes, which were taken during the walk and are accurate to what he said.
options.rationale: The error is confusing accurate transcription with shared understanding. You can be word-perfect on what he said and still have taken the wrong meaning from three shift reports.

options.text: Raise it at the monthly review, where the expectations can be walked through with him properly.
options.rationale: The error is leaving unverified assumptions steering the work for a month. The review is a good place to discuss them and a poor place to first discover they were wrong.

options.text: Ask his shift supervisor to check the write-up, since he sees the reporting in daily use.
