options.rationale: The error is verifying one person's expectation with a different person. The supervisor can tell you what is practical, and he cannot confirm what the plant manager meant.

questions.explanation: The step most often skipped is showing the customer the record you made of them, and until that happens the record is a statement about your understanding rather than theirs. Circulating it costs a message and does two jobs at once: it corrects mishearings and it invites the customer to volunteer changes that have occurred since. Anything quoted upward to a sponsor should have been seen by the person it is attributed to.
questions.mindset: Show the customer what you wrote down about them before you act on it or report it.

questions.stem: Your product supports a contract electronics manufacturer that assembles circuit boards. Its priorities move every quarter and always have: new product introductions dominate before the autumn peak, yield and rework in the quiet spring. Your team experiences this as churn and has started to resist replanning. The customer is not being capricious and is simply running its own business. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Map the customer's own annual cycle and set the planning horizon around it, so the movement is anticipated rather than absorbed as disruption.
options.rationale: Predictable movement can be planned for, and doing so converts churn into a rhythm the team can prepare for. It also makes it visible when a change is not part of the pattern and deserves a harder question.

options.text: Agree with the customer what will not move within a given quarter, so predictability exists somewhere in the plan.
options.rationale: Teams need something stable to work against and customers need room to move, and a protected quarter gives both. Naming what is fixed is what makes the rest of the plan safe to change.

options.text: Ask the customer to commit to a fixed priority order for the next twelve months.
options.rationale: The error is asking a customer to be more certain than their business allows. You will get a document that is wrong by November and an expectation that they should have stuck to it.

options.text: Treat every reprioritisation as a change request so the cost of movement is visible to the customer.
options.rationale: The error is applying a control mechanism to legitimate movement. It adds friction without stopping the change and teaches the customer that telling you early is punished.

options.text: Build the top items from all four quarters now, so whichever priority arrives the capability already exists.
options.rationale: The error is pre-building against priorities known to move. Most of it is never needed in the form anticipated, and it consumes the capacity that made responsiveness possible.

questions.explanation: Some customer volatility is disorder and some is the shape of the customer's own year, and the two demand opposite responses. Where movement is structural, the plan should be built around it and the team's stability found in what has been agreed not to move, rather than in a commitment the customer cannot honestly give. Treating predictable movement as indiscipline pushes customers into concealing changes until they are unavoidable.
questions.mindset: Plan around the customer's own cycle when their priorities move for structural reasons, and find stability in what you have agreed will not move.

questions.stem: The trustee chair funding your callout and equipment system for a mountain rescue network asked at kickoff to hear about any problem by phone before it appears in a written report. Last week your team lead put a four-week slip in the monthly report, which is accurate and was issued on time. The chair read it there first and has sent you a short, cold email. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ring him now, acknowledge the channel was wrong, and agree with him what specifically triggers a call in future.
options.rationale: The apology repairs this instance and the trigger prevents the next one, which will otherwise depend on somebody's judgement under pressure. Making it a rule takes it out of the discretion that just failed.

options.text: Reply setting out that the report was accurate and issued to the agreed schedule.
options.rationale: The error is answering a complaint about how he was told with a defence of what he was told. Both facts are true and neither is what he raised.

options.text: Stop putting problems in the written report and raise them by phone instead, as he prefers.
options.rationale: The error is replacing the record with a conversation. He asked to hear first, not instead, and a project with no written record of its problems is worse governed for everyone including him.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to remind him that the monthly report is the agreed formal reporting channel.
options.rationale: The error is enforcing your process over an explicit expectation you accepted at kickoff. Being technically compliant with the reporting schedule is not worth what it costs with a funder.

questions.explanation: Customers hold expectations about the manner and sequence of communication, particularly about bad news, and these are breached by accurate reporting all the time. Because such preferences are honoured by discretion they fail exactly when everyone is busy, so the durable repair is a stated trigger rather than a renewed intention. Hearing first is also not hearing instead: the phone call precedes the record and does not replace it.
questions.mindset: Where a customer has asked to hear bad news a particular way, make it a stated trigger rather than a matter of judgement.

questions.stem: Six weeks after handover of a production reporting system to an injection moulding toolmaker, three separate requests have come in from the same customer. Each looks superficially like a fault in your work, and the customer expects all three to be fixed free of charge. Match each situation to the route that properly applies to it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A cycle time report totals incorrectly because the calculation does not do what the agreed acceptance criteria specify.
A scrap rate report is useless because the agreed acceptance criteria themselves specified the wrong basis, and both parties signed them.
The production manager now wants a tool-wear report that was never discussed at any point during the project.

options.text: Warranty correction, carried out by the supplier at no cost to the customer.
options.rationale: Work that does not meet its agreed criteria was never delivered, so putting it right completes the original obligation. Charging for it would be charging the customer for something they already bought.

options.text: A change to an agreed baseline, decided and priced through the agreed change route.
options.rationale: Both parties agreed a basis that turned out to be wrong, which is a change rather than a defect. Treating a jointly signed error as a fault in delivery makes the supplier the insurer of the customer's specification.

options.text: New work, estimated and scheduled through the support and enhancement route.
options.rationale: Nothing was ever agreed about tool wear, so there is no obligation to compare it against. The route matters more than the cost here, because it sets the precedent for the next request.

options.text: An operational query for the customer's own service desk, requiring no supplier action.
options.rationale: Not used. This is the right route for someone who cannot find a report or has misread one, and all three situations here concern what the system does rather than how it is being used.

questions.explanation: After handover, the customer experiences everything that is not right as one category, and the supplier's job is to sort it into obligations, changes and new work without arguing about goodwill each time. The line that matters is what was agreed and whether the delivery met it, which means a jointly signed mistake is a change rather than a defect. Settling these routes before handover is what stops each request becoming a negotiation.
questions.mindset: Sort every post-handover request by what was agreed and whether it was met, before considering who should pay.

questions.stem: Three things have happened this fortnight that your team has described, loosely, as the customer changing their mind. Each has a different cause, and the first move is different in each case. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A customer expectation has moved because their regulator brought forward a deadline they are obliged to meet. The right first move is to
A customer expectation has moved because one of their managers saw a competitor's product at a conference. The right first move is to
No customer expectation has actually moved, but your team has assumed one has because nobody has heard from them for six weeks. The right first move is to

options.text: re-plan with them against the new date, because the constraint is real and outside their control
options.rationale: A regulatory date is not a preference and cannot be negotiated with your backlog. Treating it as a request to be weighed wastes the time that re-planning needs.

options.text: find out which problem the competitor's feature solves for them before treating it as a request
options.rationale: What was seen is a solution, and the useful information is the need it appeared to answer. Building the feature as described copies someone else's answer to a question you have not asked.

options.text: go and ask them, because a gap in contact is your evidence problem rather than a change in what they want
options.rationale: Silence has been filled with inference, and the team is now planning against a customer position nobody holds. The cheapest correction available is a direct question.

options.text: hold the current plan and review the position at the next quarterly meeting
options.rationale: Not used. It is the plausible default and it fails all three, because each situation has information available now and a cost attached to waiting a quarter to collect it.

questions.explanation: Changing their mind covers at least three different events: an external constraint the customer cannot control, an expectation reshaped by something they have seen, and no change at all beneath a team's assumptions. Each is a different problem, and the common error is one generic response, usually deferral to the next scheduled meeting. Establishing the cause first is what makes the response proportionate.
questions.mindset: Establish why an expectation appears to have moved before deciding what to do about it, including whether it moved at all.

questions.stem: Your project is building lot tracking and settlement for a livestock market, with nine months and £400,000 remaining. Visiting the market office, you find that two clerks have built a spreadsheet that already does the settlement work your project was funded to deliver. It is working, the market manager knows, and he has not mentioned it. He has never been anything but supportive of your project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Raise it openly, assess honestly whether the remaining scope still earns its cost, and put the question to the sponsor with stopping or reshaping among the options.
options.rationale: A funded benefit that has already been realised by other means changes the business case, and only the sponsor can decide what follows. Presenting stopping as a real option is what makes the assessment credible.

options.text: Continue as planned, since a spreadsheet built by two clerks is undocumented, unsupported and a risk in itself.
options.rationale: The error is using a true statement to avoid a question. The fragility is real and it is an argument about how to replace the spreadsheet, not a reason to spend £400,000 without re-examining the case.

options.text: Ask the market manager to have the clerks stop using the spreadsheet so the project's benefit remains measurable.
options.rationale: The error is degrading the customer's working operation to protect your benefits figure. It puts the project's reported success above the outcome the project exists to produce.

options.text: Take the spreadsheet's logic into the product as a shortcut and continue to the original scope and date.
options.rationale: The error is harvesting the artefact while ignoring what its existence tells you. The clerks solving this themselves is evidence about urgency, cost and what was really needed, and none of that reaches the sponsor.

options.text: Record it as a risk to benefits realisation and raise it in the next monthly report.
options.rationale: The error is filing a fact that changes the decision as a risk that might. Benefits already realised elsewhere is not a probability, and the register is where it will sit until the money is spent.

questions.explanation: Customers meet urgent needs themselves, and finding that they have is information about the value of what remains rather than an inconvenience to be managed around. The professional response is to surface it and let the people who authorised the investment decide, including the possibility that the right answer is to stop. Reluctance here is rarely about the evidence and usually about what stopping would mean for the project and the person running it.
questions.mindset: Put evidence that the remaining work may no longer be worth its cost in front of the sponsor, including when it argues for stopping.

questions.stem: At today's review the production manager of a creamery is delighted with the new batch maturation tracker and says he will put all fourteen ripening rooms onto it next month. Your team knows the screen queries badly and will slow to a crawl beyond about four rooms, and that hardening it is perhaps three weeks of work not yet planned. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the praise, then tell him plainly what the current limit is and what you propose to do before he scales up.
options.rationale: His rollout decision is being taken now on an incomplete picture, and the limit is the one fact he needs. Pairing it with a proposal keeps it a delivery conversation rather than a confession.

options.text: Say nothing for now and get the hardening work into the next sprint so the limit never becomes visible.
options.rationale: The error is letting a customer make a commitment on a version of the product you know does not exist yet. If the work slips, he finds out by failure in fourteen rooms.

options.text: Decline the praise and explain the query performance problem and its causes in detail.
options.rationale: The error is transferring an internal engineering problem to the customer wholesale. He needs the constraint and the plan, not the architecture, and the detail will only reduce his confidence in things that are working.

options.text: Add the hardening work to the next sprint and mention the constraint at the review after it is fixed.
options.rationale: The error is fixing quietly and disclosing afterwards. He plans his rollout in the interval, and he learns nothing about how to judge what he can rely on.

questions.explanation: Praise for something a team knows to be fragile is uncomfortable and is also the best available moment to set an accurate expectation, because the customer is receptive and no dispute exists. What they need is the boundary and the plan, expressed in terms of what they can safely do, rather than the internal reasons. Silence here is not modesty: it lets the customer build commitments on a picture you know to be wrong.
questions.mindset: When a customer praises something you know is fragile, give them the boundary before they build plans on it.

questions.stem: You meet the operations director of a helicopter charter operator monthly to review the crew and aircraft scheduling programme. Three times this quarter her expectations changed shortly after a meeting and you learned of it weeks later, twice after work had been done that no longer fitted. Your instinct is to propose weekly meetings instead. Her own operational decisions are taken at a Tuesday planning call each week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Move to weekly meetings, so that no more than a week can pass before a change of expectation reaches you.
options.rationale: The error is answering a latency problem by consuming more of a senior customer's time. Attendance and preparation fall, and you end up with four thin meetings instead of one substantial one.

options.text: Set the review rhythm against where her decisions are actually made, and agree a route for expectation changes to reach you between reviews.
options.rationale: Expectations change at her Tuesday call rather than at your review, so aligning to that is what shortens the delay. The between-meetings route matters because no cadence catches everything.

options.text: Ask her to notify you whenever her expectations change, so the monthly meeting can stay as it is.
options.rationale: The error is outsourcing the tracking to the person least likely to notice. People rarely experience their own changes of view as events worth reporting, which is exactly why this keeps happening.

options.text: Keep the monthly meeting and rely on the expectations register to surface changes as they are recorded.
options.rationale: The error is trusting a register to solve a capture problem. It faithfully records what has been captured, and what has been captured is the thing that is arriving weeks late.

questions.explanation: Expectations change when the customer takes decisions, not when the project holds meetings, so a review cadence should be set against the customer's own decision rhythm rather than against a reporting calendar. Adding meetings is the reflex and it buys less than it costs, because frequency without alignment simply samples the same gap more often. Whatever the cadence, something will change between reviews, which is why a route for the interval is part of the design.
questions.mindset: Set your listening rhythm by where the customer makes decisions, not by the shape of your reporting calendar.
